Access host

  • While you can manage most aspects of Harvester through the UI, there are tasks you will need to perform using the CLI kubectl or SUSE’s CLI rancher which you can download from GitHub. Dell does not recommend running the CLI on the Harvester nodes, though it is possible if necessary. Instead, create a bastion host with rancher and/or the kubectl client of the same version as your cluster. Here we install kubectl.

    pmax30:~ # kubectl version

    Client Version: v1.33.0

    Kustomize Version: v5.6.0

    Server Version: v1.33.5+rke2r1

    After you install kubectl, download the KubeConfig file from the cluster. To do this, log in to the Harvester UI and click on the Support link at the bottom of the menu.

    Figure 23.    Support link in Harvester UI

    Next, click on the Download KubeConfig box in the Harvester Support page in Figure 24 and it will download a file named local.yaml.

    Figure 24.    Download KubeConfig

    Copy the contents of this file to the bastion server and paste into a file, for example ~/.kube/config. Set the variable KUBECONFIG to this file: export KUBECONFIG=/root/.kube/config. Now you can access the Harvester cluster:

    pmax30:~ # kubectl get nodes

    NAME                  STATUS   ROLES                       AGE   VERSION

    pmax1.harvester.com   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   13d   v1.33.5+rke2r1

    pmax4.harvester.com   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   13d   v1.33.5+rke2r1

    pmax7.harvester.com   Ready    control-plane,etcd,master   13d   v1.33.5+rke2r1

    Harvester node access

    SUSE locks down the root user on the Harvester node so you cannot log in directly. Instead, you must use the rancher user and the password you set during the installation. Once you access the Harvester node you can run sudo -i to switch to root. To save time, you can create a rancher user on the bastion server and then setup SSH equivalency across the nodes using ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id. Below is an example of using SSH to log in to a Harvester node as the rancher user without a password and then the switch to the root user.

    rancher@pmax30:~> ssh pmax7

    Last login: Mon Feb 16 01:36:56 2026 from 172.16.60.30

    rancher@pmax7:~> sudo -i

    pmax7:~ # whoami

    root

    pmax7:~ #

Document purpose

  • This document provides configuration and deployment details for implementing SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) and integrating it with SUSE Rancher Prime. It describes the installation of a Harvester cluster and the deployment of Rancher Prime running on K3s virtual machines hosted within that cluster.

    The guide covers:

    • Installation and configuration of a SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster (version 1.6.1), including:
    • Dell PowerMax CSI driver installation
    • VM creation and cloning
    • Deployment of a K3s cluster on virtual machines on Harvester to host the Rancher Prime management plane.
    • Installation of the Rancher Prime UI and CLI.
    • Deployment of the Harvester plugin within Rancher Prime.
    • Registration and centralized management of the Harvester cluster through Rancher Prime.
    • Monitoring configurations

    This document demonstrates how SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) and Rancher Prime work together to provide a Kubernetes‑native virtualization platform with centralized cluster management, using supported and released SUSE components.

    Note: The contents of this document are valid for the software and hardware versions described. For information about updated configurations for newer software and hardware versions, contact your SUSE or Dell Technologies sales representative.

External networks

  • If you need to access a VM from outside the Harvester cluster, you have several options with varying complexity. The easiest approach is to use a unique VLAN on the default cluster management network. It is also possible to add a new cluster network and then create a network configuration that utilizes unused NICs in the Harvester nodes. If you have multiple NICs attached to different switches, this is the most effective approach. For complex requirements, SUSE offers experimental features through Kube-OVN.

    In our environment, we add a secondary VLAN to the cluster management network (our setup uses VLAN 60 for the installation) on each Harvester node. Once available we then create a virtual machine network. These procedures follow next.

    Adding a secondary VLAN to the management network

    To add a secondary VLAN, you must modify two sections of the /oem/90_custom.yaml file on each node and reboot. If you do not modify every node in the cluster, it will limit where the VMs can run. Before beginning, take a backup of the current file so you can revert to it if the node fails to come back up after reboot.

    Step 1

    In 90_custom.yaml find the line with the setup_bond.sh file. Add a new line below the existing bridge as in bold below, using the new VLAN number.

        - path: /etc/wicked/scripts/setup_bond.sh

                  permissions: 493

                  owner: 0

                  group: 0

                  content: |

                    #!/bin/sh

                    ACTION=$1

                    INTERFACE=$2

                    case $ACTION in

                            post-up)

                                    # inherit MAC address

                                    ip link set dev mgmt-br address $(ip -json link show dev $INTERFACE | jq -j '.[0]["address"]')

                                    #skip bridge vlan setting when no vlan id or vlan id=1 specified by user

                                    if [ 60 -eq 0 ] || [ 60 -eq 1 ]; then

                                        exit 0

                                    fi

                                    #assign user configured vlan,PVID=1 by default

                                    bridge vlan add vid 60 dev $INTERFACE

                                    bridge vlan add vid 70 dev $INTERFACE

                                    ;;

    Step 2

    In 90_custom.yaml find the line with the setup_bridge.sh file. Add two new lines below the existing bridge as in bold below, using the new VLAN number.

    - path: /etc/wicked/scripts/setup_bridge.sh

                  permissions: 493

                  owner: 0

                  group: 0

                  content: |

                    #!/bin/sh

                    ACTION=$1

                    INTERFACE=$2

                    case $ACTION in

                            pre-up)

                                    # enable vlan-aware

                                    ip link set $INTERFACE type bridge vlan_filtering 1

                                    ;;

                            post-up)

                                    #skip bridge vlan setting when no vlan id or vlan-id=1 specified by user

                                    if [ 60 -eq 0 ] || [ 60 -eq 1 ]; then

                                        exit 0

                                    fi

                                    #assign user configured vlan,PVID=1 by default

                                    bridge vlan add vid 60 dev $INTERFACE self

                                    bridge vlan add vid 60 dev mgmt-bo

                                    bridge vlan add vid 70 dev $INTERFACE self

                                    bridge vlan add vid 70 dev mgmt-bo

                                    ;;

    Step 4

    Reboot each node in succession, ensuring that each comes up before rebooting the next.

    VM network

    After the VLAN is set on each node, you can create a new VM network.

    Step 1

    Navigate to Virtualization Management -> Harvester Clusters -> <your cluster hyperlink> -> Networks -> Virtual Machine Networks and click Create.

    Figure 68.    Step 1 – VM network

    Step 2

    In the Basics tab choose a Namespace, Name, and Description if desired. Use the drop-down to select L2VlanNetwork, set the Vlan ID to the newly added one, and use the drop-down to select the mgmt Cluster Network. Continue to the next step.

    Figure 69.    Step 2 – VM network

    Step 3

    Select the Route tab and enter in the Route Mode, either DHCP or Manual. Click Create to complete.

    Figure 70.    Step 3 – VM network

    The network is now available to assign to VMs as in Figure 71.

    Figure 71.    Rocky VM with new VLAN network to facilitate external access

    Note that if you use a VLAN during the installation, and you wish to access VMs externally on that VLAN, you can create a VM network for it. Remember that the default cluster management network does not use a VLAN.

Grafana monitoring

  • Harvester Prime includes an integrated monitoring stack built around Prometheus and Grafana, providing administrators with immediate visibility into cluster‑level and VM‑level performance without requiring additional setup. When accessing Grafana through the Rancher Prime interface, the landing page offers an at‑a‑glance overview of global resource usage—CPU, memory, and storage—which serves as a quick health snapshot of the Harvester environment.

    Figure 72.    Grafana Home dashboard

    Grafana offers a set of built‑in dashboards in Figure 73 that exposes metrics collected by Prometheus from the Harvester nodes, KubeVirt workloads, and underlying infrastructure components like Kubernetes and Rancher.

    Figure 73.    Grafana available dashboards

    These dashboards offer clear breakdowns of node conditions, VM performance, network throughput, and storage activity. The Harvester Virtual Machine dashboard, in particular, provides detailed visibility into individual VM utilization patterns and lifecycle events sourced directly from KubeVirt and node exporters, making it easy to troubleshoot resource bottlenecks or confirm workload behavior.

     

    Figure 74.    Harvester VM dashboard

    Together, this out‑of‑the‑box monitoring integration gives operators a unified, consistent, and easily navigable view into the health and performance of their Harvester deployment.

Image create

  • To install a new operating system on a VM, you first must upload that ISO to an image on Harvester.

    Step 1

    Navigate to your Harvester cluster previously shown in Figure 38. Then continue navigation to Images and click Create.

    Figure 45.    Step 1 – Image create

    Step 2

    Select a Namespace, Name, and if desired enter a Description. Choose the radio button under Basics and supply the required information. In this example we pull the Rocky ISO directly from their download site. Finally, be sure that under the Storage tab, the Storage Class is harvester-longhorn. If you set the PowerMax storage class as default, it will use that unless you change it. Harvester only support harvester-longhorn for images. Click Create.

    Figure 46.    Step 2 – Image create

    The image downloads into the volume – see inset in Figure 47 – until it enters the active state and is available for use in a VM.

    Figure 47.    Rocky image

Home > Storage > PowerMax and VMAX > White Papers > SUSE Virtualization and Rancher Prime Integration with Dell PowerMax > Installation steps

Installation steps

  • The installation of Harvester is straightforward. Before starting, we recommend you complete the following:

    • Configure NTP server
    • Configure DNS server
    • Configure DHCP server if applicable
    • Download the Harvester 1.6.1 ISO file

    On one of the servers, boot to the Harvester ISO file, harvester-v1.6.1-amd64.iso, then follow these steps to create the initial cluster. This differs slightly from adding a cluster node which follows.

    The installer is text-based rather than graphical. Use a keyboard for navigation. The Tab key presents any options in the field, the arrow keys move between fields, and the Enter key will execute and move to the next screen in the wizard.

    Step 1

    After booting through the GRUB menu, the first screen asks to choose an installation mode. For the first node, select Create a new Harvester cluster and click Enter.

    Figure 5.   Step 1 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 2

    Select the Installation disk and Data disk where Harvester stores VM data when using the default Longhorn CSI. In this example in Figure 6, we use a second available device on the node (whether local or FC). If a second disk is unavailable, the Data disk may share the installation disk as in the inset in the figure. Note that you cannot use a device from the PowerMax array you will configure with the CSI driver. See the Zoning section for more detail as to why this is the case. Click Enter to continue.

    Figure 6.   Step 2 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 3

    Enter a HostName and click Enter.

    Figure 7.   Step 3 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 4

    Using Tab, select the Management NIC – in this example two – and configure the network settings. The IPv4 method will default to DHCP, though here we use Static. If you do use DHCP, be sure the node’s IP will not change once acquired. You also must add the option for routers. See the SUSE Virtualization documentation in the References for more detail. Note that if the network fails to configure with a yip error, you may have to restart the installer.

    Figure 8.   Step 4 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 5

    In step 5 you can configure the cluster network if desired. It is optional as it will default. Unless the default values conflict with your network, Dell recommends leaving these fields blank. Click Enter to proceed.

    Figure 9.   Step 5 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 6

    Add your DNS Servers and click Enter.

    Figure 10.    Step 6 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 7

    In step 7 configure the VIP Mode and VIP. If using DHCP enter the MAC address associated with the persistent IP. Click Enter.

    Figure 11.    Step 7 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 8

    Provide a Cluster token and record it. Each subsequent node in the cluster uses this token to join. Click Enter.

    Figure 12.    Step 8 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 9

    The Harvester nodes block SSH access to the root user. Instead, it uses the rancher user and once logged in, you can run sudo to access the root shell. It is the Password for the rancher user you set next, though the installer does not indicate this. Click Enter.

    Figure 13.    Step 9 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 10

    Enter the NTP Servers and click Enter.

    Figure 14.    Step 10 – Create a Harvester cluster

    Step 11

    There are three additional screens, but they are all optional, so we bundle them into a single step. If they do not apply, click Enter on each screen to compete.

    • Optional: configure proxy
    • Optional: import SSH keys
    • Optional: remote Harvester config

    Step 12

    The final screen in Figure 15 prompts for your confirmation to move forward. Click Enter to proceed with the default “Yes” value. The installer will spool the installation to the screen so you can watch the progress. The installation does take some time to complete, and it will reboot upon completion.

    Figure 15.    Harvester cluster confirmation

    After returning from reboot, the Statuses of both the Harvester Cluster and the Node in Figure 16 are in a “Setting up…” state. After a few minutes, both Statuses should enter a “Ready” state. If a Status is “Not Ready” you will need to investigate the underlying issue, though this is far more common post-installation when you update the custom files and you reboot the node. See the Troubleshooting section for more information.

    Figure 16.    Harvester post-install configuration

    Additional nodes

    After you successfully install the first node and the cluster is in a “Ready” state, you can install additional nodes – two more in this implementation. The installation proceeds similarly as the initial one, though a few screens differ so we have them below. When a step is different than the first node, we include it, otherwise the step will cross-reference the figure from the first installation.

    Step 1

    After booting through the GRUB menu, the first screen asks to choose an installation mode. For any additional node, select Join an existing Harvester cluster and click Enter.

    Figure 17.    Step 1 – Join an existing Harvester cluster

    Step 2

    Choose an installation role. If you are building a three node cluster, select Management Role for each additional node. This ensures the best high-availability.

    Figure 18.    Step 2 – Join an existing Harvester cluster

    Steps 3-6

    These steps are the same as the first node.

    • Installation disk
    • Network
    • Hostname
    • DNS

    Step 7

    Enter in the cluster Management address. This is the address provided in Figure 11.

    Figure 19.    Step 7 – Join an existing Harvester cluster

    Step 8

    Type in the Cluster token from Figure 12. Be sure it matches the first node. If it differs in any way, the node will never join the cluster, and you must reinstall it.

    Figure 20.    Step 8 – Join an existing Harvester cluster

    Steps 9-12

    These steps are the same as the first node.

    • Node password
    • NTP
    • Optional:
    • Optional: configure proxy
    • Optional: import SSH keys
    • Optional remote Harvester config
    • Confirmation screen

    That completes the additional node. Unlike the first node, you can install additional nodes simultaneously, if desired.

    Scaling

    Harvester cluster expansion is straightforward. The process to add a node mirrors the additional node installation above, allowing you to scale workers to manage increased VM and containerized workloads.

Introduction

  • The following sections cover the requirements for implementing Harvester. This assumes a bare-metal, three-node HA implementation. Harvester also supports a single-node cluster as well as using VMs (e.g., VMware) as hosts, but the requirements and installation varies from bare-metal. Please refer to the SUSE documentation.

Multipathing

  • The base installation of a Harvester node does not enable multipathing. Dell recommends enabling it with the PowerMax CSI driver, regardless of protocol. Since Harvester nodes run on SUSE Linux Micro/Elemental, which is an immutable operating system, to enable multipathing you must modify or add files in the /oem directory of each node. You cannot simply start the multipath daemon and change the /etc/multipath.conf file on the nodes as upon reboot it will return to the original state. Rather than modifying the single 90_custom.yaml, we add two new files to keep the custom file pristine. Create the following two files and place them in the /oem directory. Note that if you change the file names, be sure to keep the 99_ prefix.:

    99_multipathd.yaml

    stages:

      boot:

      - name: multipath

        systemctl:

          enable:

          - multipathd

          start:

          - multipathd

    99_multipathconf.yaml

    stages:

      initramfs:

      - name: "Configure multipath for PowerMax"

        files:

        - path: /etc/multipath.conf

          permissions: 0644

          owner: 0

          group: 0

          content: |

            defaults {

              polling_interval      5

              checker_timeout       15

              disable_changed_wwids yes

              find_multipaths       no

            }

            devices {

              device {

                vendor                   "EMC"

                product                  "SYMMETRIX"

                detect_prio              "yes"

                path_selector            "service-time 0"

                path_grouping_policy     "group_by_prio"

                path_checker             tur

                failback                 immediate

                fast_io_fail_tmo         5

                no_path_retry            3

                rr_min_io_rq             1

                max_sectors_kb           1024

                dev_loss_tmo             10

              }

            }

    After creating the files, you have two options: reboot or activate. Dell recommends rebooting the node to ensure the files work as expected. If this is not possible, you can create the /etc/multipath.conf file and then enable and start the multipath daemon. Though this does avoid a reboot, if there is any issue with the files you will not know until after a reboot when you are actively using multipath. This is why a reboot is preferable.

Overview

  • SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) is a Kubernetes-based virtualization platform that enables the deployment and management of virtual machines using cloud-native primitives. Built on upstream Kubernetes, KubeVirt, and Longhorn, Harvester provides a unified platform for running virtualized workloads alongside Kubernetes clusters using a consistent operational model.

    By using Kubernetes as the control plane, SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) exposes virtualization resources through standard Kubernetes APIs and custom resources. This allows infrastructure teams to manage compute, storage, and networking by defining the desired state in Kubernetes manifests (YAML), while maintaining compatibility with existing Kubernetes tooling and workflows.

    Key characteristics of SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) include:

    • Kubernetes-Native Virtualization: Define, schedule, and manage virtual machines as Kubernetes resources, enabling consistent lifecycle management.
    • Integrated Storage and Networking: Includes built-in distributed storage and software-defined networking to support VM workloads without external dependencies.
    • Centralized Management with Rancher Prime: When integrated with Rancher Prime, you can register and manage Harvester clusters alongside other Kubernetes environments from a single control plane.
    • Open and Extensible Architecture: Built entirely on open-source components, providing flexibility in deployment models.

    Together, SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) and Rancher Prime provide a foundation for operating virtual machines and Kubernetes clusters using shared infrastructure and governance patterns, supporting organizations adopting Kubernetes-centric infrastructure operations.

Persistent volumes

  • A Persistent Volume (PV) represents a storage resource that you provision for use within a cluster. It abstracts the underlying storage system, allowing workloads to consume storage without managing implementation details. Unlike ephemeral volumes, a PV remains available after you delete pods, ensuring data persists across pod lifecycles. In this solution, Dell PowerMax serves as the persistent storage backend, delivering enterprise-grade performance and reliability for PVs.

    StorageClass

    A StorageClass defines the parameters and provisioner that Kubernetes uses to create PVs dynamically. When you create a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and specify a StorageClass, Kubernetes provisions a PV that matches the class’s configuration—such as disk type, replication policy, or with Dell PowerMax, service level. By leveraging a StorageClass configured for Dell PowerMax, Kubernetes can automatically allocate high-performance, fault-tolerant storage resources, enabling dynamic, policy-driven storage allocation, and decoupling application requirements from physical infrastructure.

    When you create a Harvester cluster, the installer adds a number of storage classes based on the provisioner driver.longhorn.io (Longhorn V1 (CSI)). The default storage class is harvester-longhorn. When you create a PVC/PV and specify this storage class, Harvester creates the volume on the Data disk you specified during the installation. Though there are some objects that require harvester-longhorn, such as VM images, for virtual machine disks, we want to take advantage of the performance of the Dell PowerMax.

    You can create a PowerMax storage class through the CLI (kubectl) or use the Rancher Prime console; however because the UI will only surface the Longhorn provisioner, you will still need to edit the YAML manually. We cover both UI and CLI below.

    Rancher Prime UI

    Step 1

    Navigate to Virtualization Management -> Harvester Clusters and click on your cluster hyperlink (e.g., pmax-cluster).

    Figure 38.    Step 1a – PowerMax default storage class

    After clicking the hyperlink, continue the navigation to Advanced -> StorageClasses in the left-hand menu. In the right-hand panel click on Create. The installer-created storage classes will be present.

    Figure 39.    Step 1b – PowerMax default storage class

    Step 2

    You can provide a Name and Description in the screen and manually add the three mandatory parameters for PowerMax: SRP, SYMID, and ServiceLevel. Note that you cannot change the Provisioner as only one is available. When complete, click Edit as YAML.

    Figure 40.    Step 2 – PowerMax  default storage class

    Step 3

    Figure 41 shows the configuration based on the few parameters added in step 2.

    Figure 41.    Step 3a – PowerMax  default storage class

    From here, make the following alterations:

    • Change the provisioner to csi-powermax.dellemc.com
    • Remove the extraneous entries, in particular _clone: true.
    • Add fields for the default storage class:
    • storageclass.beta.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: 'true'
    • storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: 'true'

    Review the YAML in Figure 42 and click Create.

    Figure 42.    Step 3b – PowerMax  default storage class

    The new PowerMax default storage class is available for use below.

    Figure 43.    PowerMax  default storage class

    CLI via kubectl

    If you prefer to use CLI, kubectl, you can use the same or similar YAML file as the UI. In the example below, we create a storage class for OS boot volumes using a Bronze service level since we do not require a high level of performance for those. Additionally, the volumeBindingMode is WaitForFirstConsumer rather than immediate.

    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: StorageClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax-bronze-boot

      annotations:

        field.cattle.io/description: PowerMax FC Bronze SL for OS boot volumes

    allowVolumeExpansion: true

    parameters:

      SRP: SRP_1

      SYMID: '000120002164'

      ServiceLevel: Bronze

    provisioner: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    reclaimPolicy: Delete

    volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

    Figure 44.    Storage class via YAML

PowerMax

  • The PowerMax family represents the flagship products of the Dell Technologies enterprise storage business. It is a multi-node, active/active scale-out architecture using industry standard, end-to-end NVMe components. The platform features inline, global deduplication and compression, providing customers with high storage efficiency even as the system scales. The PowerMax family also provides what many consider to be the gold standard in data services, proven high availability and resiliency, and advanced security that adheres to stringent government regulations and corporate compliance requirements, such as FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3. A core strength of the PowerMax family is its ability to consolidate workloads. One can use a single PowerMax system to consolidate from one-to-many types of workloads, and both block and file storage services.

    PowerMax systems are modular, enabling them to expand to meet the future needs of the customer. The PowerMax family of arrays has four models:

    • PowerMax 2500 with a maximum capacity of 8 PBe (Petabytes effective)
    • PowerMax 2000 with a maximum capacity of 1.2 PBe
    • PowerMax 8500 with a maximum capacity of 18 PBe
    • PowerMax 8000 with a maximum capacity of 4.5 PBe

    Dell configures the PowerMax at the factory with a single Storage Resource Pool, or SRP, which is comprised of the physical disks in the array, managed as data pools. The array uses these collection of data pools for capacity and performance management. All host devices are part of an SRP.

    PowerMax for Open Systems provides support for the following protocols:

    • Fiber-Channel (FC) and NVMe over FC (NVMe/FC) with speeds of 8 Gb/s, 16 Gb/s, or 32 Gb/s
    • iSCSI and NVMe over TCP (NVMe/TCP) with speed of 10 Gb/s or 25 Gb/s
    • SRDF over FC with speed of 8 Gb/s, 16 Gb/s, or 32 Gb/s
    • SRDF over IP with speed of 10 Gb/s or 25 Gb/s

    PowerMaxOS operating system

    PowerMaxOS is the advanced operating system that powers Dell PowerMax storage arrays, delivering a software-defined, performance-optimized platform designed for mission-critical enterprise workloads. It is a modern architecture that is modular, container-based, and tightly integrated with end-to-end NVMe hardware to offer ultra-low latency, high throughput, and automated efficiency.

    Built with intelligent machine learning, PowerMaxOS dynamically analyzes I/O patterns to optimize data placement and resource usage in real time. It supports inline compression and de-duplication, ensuring space efficiency. With native encryption, secure snapshots, and multi-tenancy features, PowerMaxOS also ensures strong data protection and isolation.

    PowerMax replication

    PowerMax local replication includes TimeFinder/SnapVX (snapshots) and TimeFinder/Clone (clones), while PowerMax remote replication includes the SRDF product line. TimeFinder provides point-in-time local replication and data protection, and SRDF provides continuous remote replication, high availability, and disaster recovery.

    You can initiate or restore PowerMax TimeFinder snapshots or clones on SRDF target devices. One benefit of this integration is that it allows the creation of remote copies of the source application without interrupting remote replication. If the source application data is corrupted, the remote snapshot (or clone) and SRDF can restore the data in parallel to the source volumes. SRDF sends only changed data during normal operation and utilizes write folding to reduce the network impact.

Home > Storage > PowerMax and VMAX > White Papers > SUSE Virtualization and Rancher Prime Integration with Dell PowerMax > PowerMax CSI

PowerMax CSI

  • The Container Storage Interface, or CSI, is an industry standard for exposing block and file storage to containerized applications like Kubernetes, a Container Orchestration System. The CSI drivers implement an interface between CSI-enabled Container Orchestrator (CO) and storage arrays. It is a plug-in you install into Kubernetes to provide persistent storage using a Dell storage system like PowerMax. The PowerMax CSI driver supports most protocols, capabilities, and access modes. Please see the Dell documentation here for details.

    Container Storage Modules enhance the CSI to provide advanced enterprise storage features for Kubernetes clusters. It includes software modules that extend beyond CSI, offering enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes users. These modules are Authorization, Replication, Snapshotting, Resiliency and Observability.

    Note: The PowerMax CSI driver 1.16.1 does not support the use of the Container Storage Modules with SUSE Virtualization. Dell will add CSM support in a future release.

    The CSI driver installation instructions vary depending on the underlying Kubernetes environment. When installing on SUSE Virtualization, you can use the CSM Operator, Helm, or install it offline. We use the Operator in this configuration. You should implement the CSI driver from the bastion server.

    Note: When implementing the PowerMax CSI driver, we use Fibre Channel, which is the most common protocol on the PowerMax platform. You can also use iSCSI or NVMeoF as protocols if preferred.

    CSM Operator

    Follow these steps to install the CSM Operator.

    Step 1

    If necessary, install the volume snapshot CRDs. By default these should already be part of the Harvester nodes so you should not need to install them. Run the following command to view the CRDs on your nodes.

    pmax30:~ # kubectl get crds|grep volumesnap

    volumesnapshotclasses.snapshot.storage.k8s.io

    volumesnapshotcontents.snapshot.storage.k8s.io

    volumesnapshots.snapshot.storage.k8s.io      

    Step 2

    Clone and checkout the required csm-operator version using this command.

    git clone -b v1.11.0 https://github.com/dell/csm-operator.git

    When complete, change directories to csm-operator.

    cd csm-operator

    Step 3

    Execute the following command to install the operator.

    bash scripts/install.sh

    The output will be similar to Figure 36. You can ignore the warnings about the Kubernetes version.

    Figure 36.    CSM operator installation

    Validate the installation by executing the following command. There should be a single pod running:

    kubectl get pods -n dell-csm-operator

    NAME                                                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS  

    dell-csm-operator-controller-manager-6bfc7f675f-ht6hb   1/1     Running   0         

    After a successful installation, proceed with the CSI installation.

    CSI installation

    Dell provides documentation on the installation of the PowerMax CSI driver which you can locate at this link. This documentation may vary based on the CSM version. As of this writing, the current version is 1.16.1 which is the first version to support SUSE Virtualization. We include the steps below for ease of reference; however, always refer to the official documentation.

    Reverse Proxy

    Unlike the other Dell CSI drivers, the PowerMax requires a Reverse Proxy. The function of the proxy is to regulate the REST API calls sent to the Unisphere instance. It can queue these requests to enhance the performance of the driver.

    Step 1

    Install the certificate manager:

    kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.16.1/cert-manager.yaml

    Step 2

    Create an SSL certificate and private key. You will supply this later in the installation when creating a TLS secret.

    Generate a configuration file (e.g., openssl.cnf). Here is an example. You can use this without modification if you wish.

    [ req ]

    default_bits       = 2048

    distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name

    req_extensions     = req_ext

    prompt             = no

    [ req_distinguished_name ]

    C  = XX

    L  = Default City

    O  = Default Company Ltd

    [ req_ext ]

    subjectAltName = @alt_names

    [ alt_names ]

    DNS.1 = "csipowermax-reverseproxy"

    IP.1 = "0.0.0.0"

    On a Linux host with openssl, generate the certificate and private key. Be sure to note the location as you will use them in a later step.

    openssl genrsa -out tls.key 2048

    openssl req -new -key tls.key -out tls.csr -config openssl.cnf

    openssl x509 -req -in tls.csr -signkey tls.key -out tls.crt -days 3650 -extensions req_ext -extfile openssl.cnf

    Zoning

    Complete zoning of the hosts to the array according to the best practices in the section FC connectivity. It is important to validate that the initiators are on the fabric and logged into the array, but that no host groups exist. The CSI driver creates the hosts through the REST API and if they exist, the installation will fail. This is also why it is not possible to present storage from the CSI PowerMax array to the Harvester nodes for use as the Data disk previously shown in Figure 6. If not sharing the Installation disk, the Data disk must be from another PowerMax array or other storage source.

    CSI driver installation

    Step 1

    Create a namespace for the driver:

    kubectl create namespace powermax

    Step 2

    Create the PowerMax credentials. In this file you specify the array, Unisphere for PowerMax environment for endpoints and management servers, and supply the username and password.

    Note: If you skip the certificate validation (true) do not include the certsecret field or the CSI driver will fail to deploy. The installation looks for the existence of the certificate secret even if you tell it not to validate it.

    cat << EOF > secret.yaml

    storageArrays:

      - storageArrayId: "0001200012164"

        primaryEndpoint: https://172.16.60.20:8443

        backupEndpoint: https://172.16.60.21:8443

    managementServers:

      - endpoint: https://172.16.60.20:8443

        username: smc

        password: smc

        skipCertificateValidation: true

      - endpoint: https://172.16.60.21:8443

        username: smc

        password: smc

        skipCertificateValidation: true

    EOF

    Create the secret with the following command:

    kubectl create secret generic powermax-creds --namespace powermax --from-file=config=secret.yaml

    Step 3

    Create the Reverse Proxy secret using the file you generated in the section Reverse Proxy.

    kubectl create secret -n powermax tls csirevproxy-tls-secret --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key

    Step 4

    The last step is to create the PowerMax custom resource. Below is a minimal example configuration file which requires very few modifications in the envs section. Note that the variable X_CSI_REVPROXY_USE_SECRET must be set to true.

    apiVersion: storage.dell.com/v1

    kind: ContainerStorageModule

    metadata:

      name: powermax

      namespace: powermax

    spec:

      version: v1.16.0

      driver:

        csiDriverType: "powermax"

        forceRemoveDriver: true

        common:

          envs:

            - name: "X_CSI_REVPROXY_USE_SECRET"

              value: "true"

            - name: X_CSI_MANAGED_ARRAYS

              value: "0001200012164"

            - name: X_CSI_POWERMAX_PORTGROUPS

              value: ""

            - name: X_CSI_TRANSPORT_PROTOCOL

              value: ""

      # These are the modules which are optional and can be enabled by specifying to enable/disable.

      modules:

        - name: authorization

          # enable: Enable/Disable csm-authorization

          enabled: false

          components:

            - name: karavi-authorization-proxy

              envs:

                # proxyHost: hostname of the csm-authorization server

                - name: "PROXY_HOST"

                  value: "authorization-ingress-nginx-controller.authorization.svc.cluster.local"

        - name: resiliency

          enabled: false

        - name: replication

          enabled: false

        - name: observability

          # enabled: Enable/Disable observability

          enabled: false

          components:

            - name: otel-collector

              enabled: true

            - name: cert-manager

              # enabled: Enable/Disable cert-manager

              # Allowed values:

              #   true: enable deployment of cert-manager

              #   false: disable deployment of cert-manager only if it's already deployed

              # Default value: false

              enabled: false

            - name: metrics-powermax

              enabled: true

    Save the file and create the resource.

    kubectl create -f powermax_resource.yaml

    Wait for a few minutes and then check if the CR is successful with the following command. Sometimes initial errors are false-positives, and the STATE will report as Failed, but after a few minutes changes to Succeeded.

    kubectl get csm powermax -n powermax

    NAME       CREATIONTIME   CSIDRIVERTYPE   CONFIGVERSION  STATE

    powermax   5m             powermax        v1.16.0        Succeeded

    You can also log in to Unisphere for PowerMax and validate that there is a new host for each Harvester node in Figure 37. Note that if you scale your Harvester cluster, the resource will create a new host for that node automatically.

    Figure 37.    CSI-created host groups

Prerequisites

  • You must meet the following prerequisites before implementing Harvester with PowerMax.

    Server requirements for a production deployment of Harvester are as follows:

    • A minimum of three Dell servers with either an ARM64 or x86_64 architecture. In order to achieve live migration of VMs, the servers should be identical.
    • SUSE recommends 16 CPUs, 64 GB RAM, and a 500 GB disk for production. Note the disk can be internal or SAN. Dell recommends separate disks for the installation and VM repository.

            Specifically, the installation requirement is only 180 GB. The 500 GB assume the Data disk is co-resident. If you use a separate disk for Data, it must be at least 250 GB but then the installation disk could be smaller than 500 GB.

    • If you use only three servers, they should all be control-plane nodes and schedulable.
    • One 10 Gbps NIC minimum for management and one 10 Gbps NIC minimum for VM workload. For testing purposes you can utilize VM networks built on the management network and thus use a single NIC, or two bonded NICs such as detailed in this paper.
    • Port trunking for VLAN support.

    Storage requirements for SUSE Virtualization are as follows:

    • An installed PowerMax 2500 or 8500 array with a PowerMaxOS version supported by the chosen PowerMax CSI release.
    • At least four (4) front-end ports zoned to each Harvester server, preferably in one-to-one zoning to two (2) dual-ported HBAs.

    Miscellaneous requirements:

    • A bastion server from which you can issue the kubectl commands.
    • A DNS and NTP server.
    • SUSE Virtualization, “type” Prime, is a licensed solution, though there is a free Community “type.”

    You can find detailed requirements, including network port specifications, in the Harvester documentation here.

Rancher Prime

  • Rancher Prime is the enterprise offering of Rancher, though both using the same source code. The Rancher Prime UI is a central interface to manage your Harvester clusters. SUSE offers a variety of guides to deploy on many different providers, including a manual installation on a RKE2 or K3s Kubernetes cluster. In this example environment we use K3s.

    Note: If your business is federal, financial, or another highly regulated industry, SUSE recommends RKE2 over K3s because of its extensive hardening. You can find more detail on the RKE2 website.

    Environment

    The hardware requirements for a manual implementation of Rancher Prime are modest. For a small K3s Kubernetes implementation which can manage 150 clusters and 1500 nodes, four vCPUs and 16 GB of RAM are sufficient. Each small Dell 740 server in our K3s cluster setup has 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM with a 447 GB internal disk.

    Note: SUSE does not recommend deploying the Rancher Prime cluster on the Harvest cluster you intend to manage as it causes networking problems.

    Installation of K3s

    We start by installing the SLES 15 SP7 operating system on the three custom nodes in preparation for the K3s cluster. This is one of the systems SUSE supports for this. After the installation, run the following commands as root.

    Node 1

    curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | INSTALL_K3S_VERSION="v1.34.3+k3s1" sh -s - server --cluster-init

    Pull the token:

    cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/token

    Nodes 2 and 3

    Supply the token on the other nodes so they join the cluster. We use three control planes for high availability.

    curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://172.16.60.36:6443 K3S_TOKEN=K10ffeb5aaf2b1177316cd9aafd5742ffa287476452a1b133e3a42cd6efc740f9ed::server:3d93667d1ae48967bce36e6445d50c55 sh -s - server

    When complete you should have three control plane nodes.

    pmax36:~ # kubectl get nodes

    NAME     STATUS   ROLES                AGE   VERSION

    pmax36   Ready    control-plane,etcd   15d   v1.34.3+k3s1

    pmax37   Ready    control-plane,etcd   15d   v1.34.3+k3s1

    pmax38   Ready    control-plane,etcd   15d   v1.34.3+k3s1

    The cluster is ready for Rancher Prime.

    Installation of Rancher Prime

    Before installing Rancher Prime you need to create a DNS entry for the hostname you intend to use for it. That DNS entry should resolve to all three nodes in your cluster. For example, in this setup the hostname is pmax.harvester.com. Therefore in the harvester.com lookup zone, the below entries exist. After creation, proceed with the installation.

    Figure 25.    DNS entries for Rancher Prime server

    On the first node or bastion server, run the following commands to install Rancher Prime.

    Add the Rancher Prime repository

    helm repo add rancher-prime https://charts.rancher.com/server-charts/prime

    Create the cattle-system namespace 

    kubectl create namespace cattle-system

    Install the cert manager CRDs

    kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.19.2/cert-manager.crds.yaml

    Add the jetstack repository

    helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io

    Update the repositories

    helm repo update

    Install the cert manager

    helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \

      --namespace cert-manager \

      --create-namespace

    Install Rancher Prime

    helm install rancher rancher-prime/rancher \

      --namespace cattle-system \

      --set hostname=pmax.harvester.com \

      --set bootstrapPassword=admin

    Upon completion, navigate to the new hostname, in this example pmax.harvester.com, and choose a password and log in.

    Figure 26.    Rancher Prime UI initial login screen

    The home screen welcomes you to Rancher Prime and will list the deployed Kubernetes cluster housing the software as “local.”

    Figure 27.    Rancher Prime dashboard

    Harvester UI Extension

    To integrate the Harvester cluster, install the Harvester UI Extension. In the Rancher Prime UI Welcome screen, locate the left-hand panel in Figure 27, click the hamburger menu at the top. It will expand out the options in Figure 28. Click on Virtualization Management which will default to Harvester Clusters on the right. Click on the green Install button to install the extension.

    Note: The larger menu on the left will condense as soon as you click Virtualization Management.

    Figure 28.    Install Harvester UI extension

    Rancher Prime installs the latest extension, in this case 1.7.1. It is backward compatible so it will work perfectly fine with a 1.6.1 Harvester cluster as in this paper. You can downgrade if you wish, and it will show that version as current, seen in Figure 29, but the extension will show the latest.

    Figure 29.    Harvester UI extension

    Import Harvester cluster

    After installing the extension, you must import the Harvester cluster into Rancher Prime following these steps.

    Step 1

    Navigate from the Extensions page to Virtualization Management -> Harvester Clusters and click Import Existing.

    Figure 30.    Step 1 – Import Harvester cluster

    Step 2

    Enter in a Cluster Name and Cluster Description (optional). There is no name validation so choose something that distinguishes this cluster as you may have multiples. Click Create.

    Figure 31.    Step 2 – Import Harvester cluster

    Step 3

    Upon creation, Rancher Prime provides instructions on how to update the Harvester UI to complete the import. Copy the URL in step 3 in Figure 32 and open the Harvester UI.

    Figure 32.    Step 3 – Import Harvester cluster

    Step 4

    In the Harvester UI, navigate in the left-hand menu to Advanced -> Settings. Scroll down to the parameter cluster-registration-url on the right-hand panel and click the three buttons next to it.

    Figure 33.    Step 4 – Import Harvester cluster

    Step 5

    Update the value from the URL copied in Figure 32 and click Save.

    Figure 34.    Step 5 – Import Harvester cluster

    You can return to the Harvester Cluster page in Rancher Prime and watch the progression of importation. The State will move from Pending -> Waiting -> Active, each change adding more information in the table. Once Active you can click the green Manage button.

    Figure 35.    Harvester cluster activation

Snapshots

  • VM-level snaps with PowerMax volumes are storage array snapshots driven through the CSI driver utilizing TimeFinder/SnapVX on the Dell PowerMax. TimeFinder/SnapVX, or SnapVX, is a local replication solution that creates point-in-time copies, or snapshots, of PowerMax devices. SnapVX creates snapshots by storing changed tracks (deltas) directly in the SRP of the source volume. With SnapVX, you do not need to specify a target volume and source/target pairs when you create a snapshot. If the application ever needs to use the point-in-time data, you can create links from the snapshot to one or more target volumes. If there are multiple snapshots and the application needs to find a particular point-in-time copy for host access, you can link and relink until the correct snapshot is located. Snapshots are crash-consistent copies of the data.

    csi-driver-config

    By default, Harvester does not support taking snapshots of VMs that use external storage like the PowerMax, only VMs with longhorn volumes. To allow external storage you must modify an advanced parameter either in the Harvester or Rancher Prime UI. Follow these steps.

    Step 1

    Create a PowerMax volume snapshot class. There is no UI wizard so you must use kubectl on your bastion server. Here is a simple YAML for this class. You can change the name if desired. Save it to a file and create it with kubectl create -f <file>.

    apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1

    kind: VolumeSnapshotClass

    metadata:

      name: powermax-snapclass

    driver: csi-powermax.dellemc.com

    deletionPolicy: Delete

    Step 2

    Log in to the Harvester UI and navigate in the left-hand menu to Advanced -> Settings. Scroll down on the right-hand side until you reach the csi-driver-config parameter. Click the three buttons next to the parameter on the right.

    Figure 54.    Step 2 – Modify csi-driver-config

    Step 3

    Once in the dialogue, click Add.

    Figure 55.    Step 3 – Modify csi-driver-config

    Step 4

    Using the drop-down boxes, select the PowerMax provisioner for Provisioner and the volume storage class from step 1 for Volume Snapshot Class Name. There is no Backup Volume Snapshot Class Name since Harvester only supports its use with longhorn. Click Save.

    Figure 56.    Step 4 – Modify csi-driver-config

    Both snapshot classes are now available for use in Figure 57.

    Figure 57.    Modified csi-driver-config

    Once complete, you will need to wait for a few minutes before the Take Virtual Machine Snapshot menu is available for VMs with PowerMax storage.

    VM snapshot

    You can execute a snapshot from either UI interface, or through CLI. The following example uses the Rancher Prime UI.

    Step 1

    Navigate in the UI to the Virtual Machines option in the left-hand menu. Highlight the desired VM in the right-hand display and click the three buttons next to it. Select Take Virtual Machine Snapshot.

    Figure 58.    Step 1 – VM snapshot

    Step 2

    Enter in the desired name and click Create.

    Figure 59.    Step 2 – VM snapshot

    If successful, the following pop-up appears.

    Figure 60.    Successful VM snapshot

    The CSI driver acts as a bridge between the Kubernetes cluster and the storage array. When you create a VolumeSnapshot, the CSI driver sends a request to the storage array to create a snapshot of the PV. The storage array then creates the snapshot and returns a unique identifier to the CSI driver, which stores this identifier in the Kubernetes VolumeSnapshot object.

    You can query the snapshot through CLI or Unisphere for PowerMax. You can reconcile the two by viewing the SNAPSHOTCONTENT field in CLI and matching it against the Snapshot name in the UI. Here we bolded the identifier in the CLI and highlighted it in the UI to show the match.

    pmax30:~ # kubectl get volumesnapshot -n prod-vms

    NAME                                           READYTOUSE   SOURCEPVC               SOURCESNAPSHOTCONTENT   RESTORESIZE   SNAPSHOTCLASS        SNAPSHOTCONTENT                                    CREATIONTIME   AGE

    winvm1-snap-volume-winvm1-rootdisk-tjati       true         winvm1-rootdisk-tjati                           32Gi          powermax-snapclass   snapcontent-58bec62e-05f0-4334-b9ca-41fec4ed875b   13m            13m

    Figure 61.    VM snapshot reconciliation in CLI and UI

    VM restore

    Once you take a snapshot it is available for restore. You can restore it to the same VM (powered off) to undo a change or action, or you can create a new VM from it. Creating a new VM is common for testing patches or bug fixes for example. This is the use case we cover below.

    Step 1

    Navigate to Backup and Snapshots -> Virtual Machine Snapshots in the left-hand menu and click Restore Snapshot in the right-hand corner. You can also use the three buttons next to the snapshot and choose Replace Existing or Restore New.

    Figure 62.    Step 1 – VM restore

    Step 2

    The dialog defaults to Create new. Use the drop-down in the Snapshot box to select the desired snapshot. Enter a Virtual Machine Name and click Create.

    Figure 63.    Step 2 – VM restore

    If you navigate to the Virtual Machine screen you can watch as Harvester restores the VM.

    Figure 64.    VM restoring

    In Unisphere for PowerMax the snapshot now shows a link with a green checkmark to a new device which is the new VM.

    Figure 65.    Linked snapshot

Solutions Enabler

  • Solutions Enabler (SE) is a powerful command-line interface (CLI) tool designed for managing, automating, and monitoring Dell PowerMax storage systems. It provides granular control over a wide range of storage operations, including those that are unavailable in Unisphere for PowerMax. SE is especially well-suited for advanced users who require scriptable, dependable, and automation-friendly interfaces for enterprise-scale storage environments. Administrators can use SE to provision storage, manage replication (including SRDF and SnapVX), configure access control via masking views, and pull real-time performance and health metrics.

    Installed on a Windows, Linux, or UNIX management host, SE can communicate with arrays using either in-band (via HBA) or out-of-band (over IP) connections. It is frequently used in automated workflows, batch jobs, and integrations with orchestration platforms such as Ansible.

Summary

  • SUSE Virtualization, powered by Harvester and centrally managed through SUSE Rancher Prime, provides a modern, open, and flexible platform for consolidating virtual machines and Kubernetes-based workloads across hybrid environments. Its lightweight, integrated architecture simplifies operations while maintaining strong security and high availability. When combined with Dell PowerMax storage, organizations gain enterprise‑class performance and reliable data services—including advanced replication, data protection, and predictable scalability—ensuring a robust foundation for mission‑critical workloads.

    This paper outlines the configuration and deployment of SUSE Virtualization on Dell servers backed by PowerMax storage, demonstrating how the platform can efficiently support both traditional virtual machines and cloud‑native infrastructure through Rancher Prime. By following the recommended design and operational practices, organizations can accelerate adoption, streamline management across their virtualized environments, and ensure a consistent, resilient, and scalable foundation for modern IT operations built on SUSE Virtualization and PowerMax.

    Network topology

    Dell PowerMax storage

    In a Harvester cluster, array storage like the Dell PowerMax provides persistent, high-performance, and reliable storage for VMs and containerized applications. Unlike ephemeral storage tied to individual nodes, array storage ensures data survives pod restarts, node failures, and scaling operations. It enables features like dynamic volume provisioning, persistent volumes, and storage classes, allowing applications to access shared storage efficiently. This is critical for stateful workloads such as databases, message queues, and enterprise applications that require consistent data availability and performance across the cluster.

    Dell PowerMax arrays provide tiered performance through service levels, which you can map to storage classes. This allows you to assign the appropriate service level to each VM or container for optimal performance.

    Service levels

    A service level is a property of a storage group, a provisioning object on the Dell PowerMax. The service level defines the maximum and minimum response times for I/O operations that involve the storage group. The minimum response time (known as the floor) defines the shortest time that each I/O operation on the storage group takes to complete. The maximum response time (known as the ceiling) defines the longest, acceptable time for any I/O operation on the storage group. PowerMax uses the floor and ceiling values to monitor whether each storage group complies with its quality-of-service criteria.

    The storage administrator can use the service levels to help ensure that lower-priority applications do not impede storage groups associated with high-priority applications. The six service levels on the PowerMax are the following, beginning with the highest priority, and shown in Figure 4:

    • Diamond
    • Platinum
    • Gold
    • Silver
    • Bronze
    • Optimized

    Figure 4.   PowerMax service levels

    Under normal operating conditions, the PowerMax ensures that the performance is commensurate with the chosen service level’s compliance range. If, however, there is contention, the PowerMax will prioritize higher service levels by limiting performance of the lower service levels. Therefore it is essential to select the storage class best suited for the performance needs of the VM disk or containerized application.

SUSE Virtualization (Harvester)

  • SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) is an enterprise Kubernetes distribution purpose-built for running and managing virtual machines using Kubernetes-native constructs. It extends upstream Kubernetes with integrated virtualization, storage, and networking components to provide a complete platform for hosting VM workloads while remaining fully aligned with Kubernetes operational models.

    A Harvester cluster consists of nodes running a minimal, hardened Linux operating system that hosts the Kubernetes control plane, container runtime, and virtualization components. KubeVirt implements virtual machines and allows administrators to define and manage them as custom Kubernetes resources. This enables consistent lifecycle management through standard Kubernetes APIs and tooling.

    Each node runs the Kubelet agent, which registers the node with the Kubernetes control plane and reports resource availability and status. KubeVirt components integrate with the Kubelet and container runtime to schedule and execute virtual machines alongside other Kubernetes workloads. Virtual machine disks appear as persistent volumes and attach to workloads through Kubernetes storage abstractions.

    Harvester includes integrated cluster networking to provide pod-to-pod, VM-to-VM, and external connectivity. Software-defined networking components manage IP address allocation, service exposure, and traffic routing without relying on external network appliances. This allows virtual machines to communicate with each other and with external networks using standard Layer 2 and Layer 3 constructs.

    An integrated distributed storage layer provides persistent storage and supplies block storage volumes to virtual machines and Kubernetes workloads. Storage resources are dynamically provisioned and managed through Kubernetes storage classes, enabling consistent attachment, snapshot, and recovery operations across the cluster.

    Harvester also includes built-in monitoring, logging, and lifecycle management components that allow administrators to observe cluster health, resource utilization, and workload status. You manager cluster upgrades and configuration changes through Kubernetes-aware workflows to minimize operational disruption.

    Cluster architecture

    A SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster is composed of one or more nodes that collectively provide both control plane and workload execution capabilities.

    • Control Plane Components: Control plane services maintain the desired state of the cluster and coordinate scheduling and lifecycle operations. These components include the Kubernetes API server, controller manager, scheduler, and the etcd key-value store, which persists cluster configuration and state. Harvester-specific controllers extend the control plane to manage virtualization, storage, and networking resources.
    • Worker and Virtualization Components: Each node runs the Kubelet, container runtime, and KubeVirt components to execute workloads. The scheduler assigns virtual machines to nodes according to available CPU, memory, and storage. The virtualization layer enforces isolation and resource allocation and lets you manage VMs through Kubernetes‑native APIs.
    • Storage Services: The integrated storage layer provides distributed block storage across the cluster. Volumes reach virtual machines through persistent volume claims, allowing disks to be dynamically provisioned and attached. This architecture supports high availability and resiliency by distributing data across multiple nodes.
    • Networking Services: Harvester configures and manages cluster networking to support VM and pod communication. Networking components manage IP allocation, routing, and service exposure, enabling both internal cluster communication and external access without manual network configuration on individual nodes.

    Figure 1 illustrates a basic representation of the SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster as deployed in this document, showing the relationship between Kubernetes control plane services, virtualization components, storage, and networking.

    Figure 1.   SUSE Virtualization architecture

    SUSE Rancher Prime architecture and control plane

    SUSE Rancher Prime provides a centralized management and governance layer for Kubernetes environments across on‑premises, edge, and hybrid infrastructures. In this deployment, Rancher Prime runs on a highly available K3s management cluster hosted on virtual machines within SUSE Virtualization (Harvester).

    Rancher Prime acts as a central control plane for visibility, access control, and lifecycle coordination, while each managed cluster retains its own Kubernetes control plane and workload execution responsibilities. It integrates with downstream clusters through secure API connections rather than replacing their native control planes.

    Core functions

    • Cluster Registration and Inventory: A centralized inventory registers all managed clusters, including Harvester clusters, and displays their health, versions, and resource status.
    • Lifecycle Management: Rancher Prime coordinates upgrades, configuration changes, and add-on management using Kubernetes‑native mechanisms.
    • Access and Identity Management: Central services enforce authentication and authorization to provide consistent role‑based access control across clusters.
    • Extension and Integration: Platform extensions, such as the Harvester plugin, integrate directly into the Rancher Prime UI to provide infrastructure- and virtualization-aware management workflows.

    Control plane components

    • Rancher Management Server: Provides the web UI and API endpoints, maintaining cluster metadata, access policies, and configuration state.
    • K3s Management Cluster: A lightweight, CNCF‑certified Kubernetes distribution optimized for management workloads and hosted on Harvester.
    • Downstream Cluster Agents: Agents running in managed clusters establish secure connections back to Rancher Prime, enabling state observation, configuration enforcement, and health reporting.
    • Harvester Integration: The Harvester extension enhances Rancher Prime with native visibility and management of Harvester clusters, virtual machines, and infrastructure resources.

    Rancher Prime provides centralized visibility and lifecycle management for registered Harvester clusters.

    SUSE Rancher Prime user interface

    The SUSE Rancher Prime user interface is a browser-based management platform that provides centralized visibility and control for Kubernetes and virtualization environments. In this deployment, Rancher Prime serves as the primary operational interface for managing the SUSE Virtualization (Harvester) cluster and the virtual machines running within it.

    Rancher Prime does not replace the Kubernetes control plane of managed clusters; instead, it integrates with them through secure agents and APIs to present a unified management experience. Once you register the Harvester cluster, Rancher Prime exposes virtualization-aware views and workflows through the Harvester integration, allowing administrators to manage virtual machines and infrastructure resources alongside Kubernetes clusters from a single interface.

    Through Rancher Prime, administrators can:

    • View registered clusters and their health, status, and versions.
    • Access virtualization-specific inventory, including virtual machines, hosts, storage, and networks.
    • Perform virtual machine lifecycle operations such as creation, start, stop, restart, and deletion.
    • Perform snapshots, backups, and restores.
    • Monitor resource utilization across compute, storage, and networking.
    • Apply centralized authentication and role-based access control consistently across environments.

    Rancher Prime abstracts Kubernetes and virtualization components through its UI and treats virtual machines as managed resources accessed with the same navigation patterns as Kubernetes workloads. The interface groups capabilities into areas such as Cluster Management and Virtualization Management, giving operators a single console for managing clusters and virtual machines. Resource views show configuration details, runtime status, and events for both infrastructure and workloads. Rancher Prime runs on a K3s management cluster, separating management‑plane services from workload execution and preserving administrative access during maintenance or disruptions.

    Figure 2 shows the Rancher Prime user interface with SUSE Virtualization integration enabled, highlighting centralized cluster navigation and virtualization resource views.

    Figure 2.   Rancher Prime UI

Terminology

  • The following table provides definitions for some of the terms in this document.

    Table 1.      Terminology

    Term

    Definition

    CNI

    Container Network Interface; a Kubernetes specification used to configure pod and virtual machine networking within the cluster.

    Containers

    Containers are lightweight, executable images that package software along with all its dependencies. By virtualizing the operating system, containers can run consistently across different environments.

    Control plane

    Manages the cluster, including scheduling, monitoring, and maintaining desired state.

    CSI

    Container Storage Interface is an API that allows Kubernetes to manage storage.

    Deployment

    A Kubernetes resource that maintains an application’s life cycle.

    Elemental / SUSE Linux Micro

    The immutable Linux operating system used by SUSE Virtualization nodes to host Kubernetes, virtualization, and storage services.

    FC

    Fibre Channel

    Harvester

    Former product name for SUSE Virtualization; the terms are interchangeable in this document.

    K3s

    A lightweight, CNCF-certified Kubernetes distribution used in this deployment to host the Rancher Prime management plane.

    Kubectl

    The command line tool used with Kubernetes. For most commands, it is interchangeable with OC.

    Kubelet

    An agent that runs on each node and communicates with the control plane.

    Kubernetes

    Kubernetes is an open-source platform for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.

    KubeVirt

    A Kubernetes extension that enables virtual machines to run alongside containers by integrating KVM-based virtualization into Kubernetes.

    Longhorn

    A cloud-native, distributed block storage system used by SUSE Virtualization to provide persistent storage for virtual machines and Kubernetes workloads via the CSI interface.

    Namespace

    A way to divide cluster resources between multiple users or applications. It provides a logical partitioning of the cluster.

    NIC

    Network Interface Controller

    Nodes

    The machines that run the workloads. Sometimes synonymous with hosts.

    Operator

    A method of packaging, deploying, and managing a Kubernetes application. It enables one of the installation methods for the Dell PowerMax CSI driver.

    Pods

    The smallest deployable unit, typically containing one or more containers.

    PV

    Persistent volume

    PVC

    Persistent volume claim

    Rancher Prime

    SUSE’s enterprise Kubernetes management platform provides centralized lifecycle management, access control, and visibility for registered Kubernetes and Harvester clusters.

    VM

    Virtual Machine

    Worker node

    Nodes that run containerized workloads and/or virtual machines, depending on cluster role configuration.

Troubleshooting

  • The following sections provide troubleshooting information for common problems encountered in implementing SUSE Virtualization.

    Unavailable cluster or node

    After reboot of a Harvester node, the status of the Harvester Cluster or Node can enter a “Not Ready Status,” or it can be stuck in a “Setting up…” state. If you need to troubleshoot that status of the Harvester Cluster or Node, it is important to remember that Harvester nodes run on SUSE Linux Micro/Elemental, which is an immutable operating system. Because the OS is immutable, most system files return to their original state on every reboot unless you explicitly persist changes in the /oem directory. In other words, if you manually edit a file such as /etc/hosts on a node and then reboot at a later time, the system reinstalls the baseline image which overwrites your changes.

    While the OS itself is immutable, the /oem partition is writable and persistent, and the Harvester/Elemental boot process reads configuration files from there each time the system starts. Harvester uses cloud-init‑style YAML files in /oem to apply configuration during early boot. The primary custom file is  /oem/90_custom.yaml. You will see a second file in the directory name 99_settings.yaml which Harvester creates during the installation. It contains the NTP server.

    pmax1:# more 99_settings.yaml

    name: oem_settings

    stages:

        initramfs:

            - name: ntp

              systemctl:

                enable:

                    - systemd-timesyncd

                    - systemd-time-wait-sync

              timesyncd:

                NTP: 172.16.60.44

    During boot, Harvester processes these files and applies the configuration — including network settings, DNS, NTP, host adjustments, and kubelet settings.

    Changes to these files, or additional new files, are a common reason that the cluster or node enters a “Not Ready” state upon reboot. Even minor formatting errors in the YAML will prevent a “Ready” state. For example, we added a new custom file, 99_storage.yaml, with this content which inadvertently had the file name as the first line. That is an invalid YAML.

    99_storage.yaml

    name: storage settings

    stages:

      boot:

      - name: enable multipath

        systemctl:

          enable:

            - multipathd

          start:

            - multipathd

    Even though this file only enables and starts the multipath daemon, it prevents the entire Harvester OS from setting up properly. Harvester will not ignore the error like a regular OS starting up would do, i.e., the daemon would simply not start. To troubleshoot you need to log in to the node through the console as the rancher user. Because of the failures during boot, the password you set during the installation is no longer valid for rancher. It defaults back to “rancher.”

    Troubleshooting results in the discovery of the mapping values error in Figure 75. Since SUSE does not list the problematic file with the error, you must check all files, fix as necessary, and re-run the reconciler service until the error is gone. Once there are no errors, you can reboot as there is no way to continue the boot from this failed state.

    Figure 75.    YAML debugging

    Image storage class 

    Harvester will allow you to use a PowerMax storage class for an image (e.g., OS) via HTTP; however if you try to use that image in a VM, the volume will enter a “Not ready” state as below. This is because Harvester creates a copy of the image using a process the PowerMax CSI volume does not support. The only workaround is to delete the image with the PowerMax volume and upload a new image using the harvester-longhorn storage class. Note that Harvester does not support the use of any external CSI with images.

    Figure 76.    Image on PowerMax storage class

    Backups

    Harvester does not support VM backups that contain PowerMax storage. If you attempt a backup of a VM after configuring a valid backup target, it will fail with the following message about the provisioner:

    Figure 77.    Backup of VM with PowerMax storage

Unisphere for PowerMax

  • Unisphere for PowerMax is an HTML5 web-based application that enables you to provision, operate and maintain PowerMax, VMAX All Flash, and VMAX storage systems.

    Unisphere for PowerMax 10.3.0.x supports:

    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2500 and PowerMax 8500) running PowerMaxOS 10 (6079)
    • Storage systems (PowerMax 2000, PowerMax 8000, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running PowerMaxOS 5978
    • Storage systems (VMAX 100K, VMAX 200K, VMAX 400K, VMAX 250F, VMAX 450F, VMAX 850F, and VMAX 950F) running HYPERMAX OS 5977

    Unisphere for PowerMax also has a built-in Representational State Transfer (REST). The REST API allows you to access diagnostic, performance, and configuration data, as well as perform provisioning operations on the storage system through interfaces like the CSI driver. Full documentation for the Unisphere for PowerMax REST API is available at developer.dell.com or from the Help menu within the Unisphere for PowerMax User Interface.

Virtual Machines

  • You can use either CLI (kubectl) or the Rancher Prime UI to deploy a VM. The UI also provides the ability to compose and execute a YAML directly. To create a VM using the UI follow these steps.

    Step 1

    Within the cluster page, select Virtual Machines on the left-hand menu and then Create on the right-hand panel.

    Figure 48.    Step 1 – VM creation

    Step 2

    In the first screen, Harvester offers the ability to create single (default) or multiple instances. Use the drop-down box to choose the Namespace and then provide a Name and Description if desired. In the Basics screen set the CPU and Memory. Be aware that the memory is in GB, not MB. In this example in Figure 49, an SSHKey is set to allow easier access to the VM.

    Figure 49.    Step 2 – VM creation

    Step 3

    Select Volumes from the menu on the left. By default, disk-0 is available, but none of the options. Use this volume for the OS boot ISO. Use the drop-down box to select an Image from those previously uploaded. The size automatically defaults based on the ISO. Click the Add Volume button to specify a second disk for the boot OS. The storage class defaults to the powermax-fc as that is the default storage class but we modify it here to the powermax-bronze-boot storage class created for OS volumes.

    Figure 50.    Step 3 – VM creation

    Step 4

    Click Networks on the left-hand menu. Harvester sets a single network by default. This will put the VM on the management network so it will only be accessible by hosts on the network, specifically the nodes themselves. You can setup additional networks that are accessible outside of the cluster. Make any additional changes in the remaining menu categories on the left, and then click Create.

    Figure 51.    Step 4 – VM creation

    Upon creation, Harvester creates the volumes and boots the VM to the first volume in the boot order, or in this case the ISO volume. Harvester offers a WebVNC console via the browser so you can access and install the OS. The figure below shows the WebVNC console and inset is the Virtual Machines screen where you access it for each VM.

    Figure 52.    VM detail and WebVNC access

    Windows VM

    When installing a Windows VM the correct drivers to discover the VM disk are not available by default. Therefore Harvester offers templates which the user can specify and will supply these drivers during the install. You can see the Template field set to the windows base image in Figure 53. The machine creation proceeds just as for Linux with the ISO and boot disk. During installation you will choose the correct driver from the template options based on the Windows OS version.

    Figure 53.    Windows template ISO for drivers

VM CLI

  • There is no dedicated CLI for creating VMs in Harvester. You use standard kubectl and apply YAML files. Below is an example of listing all VMs in the prod-vms namespace.

    kubectl get vmi -n prod-vms

    NAME           AGE     PHASE     IP             NODENAME              READY

    mintvm1        6d18h   Running                  pmax1.harvester.com   True

    mintvm2        6d18h   Running   172.16.70.12   pmax7.harvester.com   True

    rocky-10-vm1   7d22h   Running   10.52.0.32     pmax1.harvester.com   True

    winvm1         8d      Running   10.52.1.37     pmax4.harvester.com   True

    winvm2         7d21h   Running   10.52.0.33     pmax1.harvester.com   True

VM clone

  • Harvester also supports taking clones of VMs with PowerMax volumes. Once again, you can use either UI interface. In this example we continue to use Rancher Prime.

    Step 1

    Navigate in the UI to the Virtual Machines option in the left-hand menu. Highlight the desired VM in the right-hand display and click the three buttons next to it. Select Clone.

    Figure 66.    Step 1 – VM clone

    Step 2

    Enter a New Virtual Machine Name and leave the rest at defaults. Click Create.

    Figure 67.    Step 2 – VM clone

    If you prefer to use kubectl to create a clone of the volume only, here is a sample script.

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

    metadata:

      name: mint-clone-test

      namespace: prod-vms

    spec:

      storageClassName: powermax-fc2

      accessModes:

        - ReadWriteOnce

      volumeMode: Block

      resources:

        requests:

          storage: 40Gi

      dataSource:

        kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

        name: mintvm2-disk-1-hdp2r

    Note that if a VM is the result of a snapshot restore, it cannot be the source of a clone.
